{{Short description|Branch of applied computer science}}
[[Image:Random Walk example.svg|thumb|right|420px|Simulation of [[Brownian Motion]] sample paths is an important tool in calculating the price of financial instruments under the [[risk-neutral measure]].]]
'''Computational finance''' is a branch of applied [[computer science]] that deals with problems of practical interest in [[finance]].<ref name=Seydel>Rüdiger U. Seydel, ''Tools for Computational Finance'', Springer; 3rd edition (May 11, 2006) 978-3540279235</ref> Some slightly different definitions are the study of [[data]] and [[algorithm]]s currently used in finance<ref name="CFRL">{{cite web|url=http://www.bracil.net/finance/|title=Computational Finance and Research Laboratory|publisher=University of Essex|access-date=2012-07-21|archive-date=2012-07-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120712015741/http://www.bracil.net/finance/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[mathematics]] of [[computer program]]s that realize financial [[mathematical model|models]] or [[system]]s.<ref name=Los>Cornelis A. Los, ''Computational Finance'' World Scientific Pub Co Inc (December 2000) {{ISBN|978-9810244972}}</ref>

Computational finance emphasizes practical [[numerical analysis|numerical methods]] rather than [[mathematical proof]]s and focuses on techniques that apply directly to [[economics|economic analyses]].<ref name=Miranda>Mario J. Miranda  and Paul L. Fackler, ''Applied Computational Economics and Finance'', The MIT Press (September 16, 2002) {{ISBN|978-0262134200}}</ref> It is an interdisciplinary field between [[mathematical finance]] and [[numerical analysis|numerical methods]].<ref name=Ugur>Omur Ugur, ''Introduction to Computational Finance'', Imperial College Press (December 22, 2008) {{ISBN|978-1848161924}}</ref> Two major areas are efficient and accurate computation of [[fair value]]s of [[security (finance)|financial securities]] and the modeling of [[stochastic]] [[time series]].<ref name=Duan>Jin-Chuan Duan, Wolfgang Karl Härdle and James E. Gentle (editors), ''Handbook of Computational Finance'', Springer (October 25, 2011) {{ISBN|978-3642172533}}</ref>

==History==
The birth of computational finance as a discipline can be traced to [[Harry Markowitz]] in the early 1950s. Markowitz conceived of the portfolio selection problem as an exercise in mean-variance optimization. This required more computer power than was available at the time, so he worked on useful algorithms for approximate solutions.<ref name=Markowitz>Harry M. Markowitz, ''Portfolio Selection: Efficient Diversification of Investments'', Wiley, second edition (September 3, 1991) 978-1557861085</ref> Mathematical finance began with the same insight, but diverged by making simplifying assumptions to express relations in simple [[closed-form expression|closed forms]] that did not require sophisticated computer science to evaluate.<ref name=Fox>Justin Fox, ''The Myth of the Rational Market: A History of Risk, Reward, and Delusion on Wall Street'',  HarperBusiness (June 9, 2009) {{ISBN|978-0060598990}}</ref>

In the 1960s, hedge fund managers such as [[Edward O. Thorp|Ed Thorp]]<ref name=Poundstone>William Poundstone, ''Fortune's Formula: The Untold Story of the Scientific Betting System That Beat the Casinos and Wall Street'', Hill and Wang (September 19, 2006) {{ISBN|978-0809045990}}</ref> and [[Michael Goodkin]] (working with Harry Markowitz, [[Paul Samuelson]] and [[Robert C. Merton]])<ref name=Goodkin>Michael Goodkin, ''The Wrong Answer Faster: The Inside Story of Making the Machine that Trades Trillions'', Wiley, (February 21, 2012) {{ISBN|978-1118133408}}
</ref> pioneered the use of computers in [[arbitrage]] trading. In academics, sophisticated computer processing was needed by researchers such as [[Eugene Fama]] in order to analyze large amounts of financial data in support of the [[efficient-market hypothesis]].<ref name=Fox />

During the 1970s, the main focus of computational finance shifted to [[valuation of options|options pricing]] and analyzing [[mortgage loan|mortgage]] [[securitization]]s.<ref name=Brown>Aaron Brown, ''Red-Blooded Risk: The Secret History of Wall Street'', Wiley (October 11, 2011) {{ISBN|978-1118043868}}</ref> In the late 1970s and early 1980s, a group of young [[quantitative analyst|quantitative practitioners]] who became known as "rocket scientists" arrived on [[Wall Street]] and brought along [[personal computer]]s. This led to an explosion of both the amount and variety of computational finance applications.<ref name=Ehlers>John F. Ehlers, ''Rocket Science for Traders'', Wiley (July 20, 2001) {{ISBN|978-0471405672}}</ref> Many of the new techniques came from [[signal processing]] and [[natural language processing|speech recognition]] rather than traditional fields of [[computational economics]] like [[mathematical optimization|optimization]] and [[time series]] analysis.<ref name=Ehlers />

By the end of the 1980s, the winding down of the [[Cold War]] brought a large group of displaced [[physicist]]s and [[applied mathematics|applied mathematicians]], many from behind the [[Iron Curtain]], into finance. These people became known as "[[Financial engineering|financial engineers]]" ("quant" is a term that includes both rocket scientists and financial engineers, as well as quantitative portfolio managers).<ref name=Brown1>Aaron Brown, ''The Poker Face of Wall Street'', Wiley (March 31, 2006) 978-0470127315</ref> This led to a second major extension of the range of computational methods used in finance, also a move away from personal computers to [[mainframe computer|mainframes]] and [[supercomputer]]s.<ref name=Brown /> Around this time computational finance became recognized as a distinct academic subfield. The first degree program in computational finance was offered by [[Carnegie Mellon University]] in 1994.<ref name=CM>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.cmu.edu/CCF/index.html|title= Center for Computational Finance|publisher=Carnegie Mellon University|access-date=2012-07-21 }}</ref>

Over the last 20 years, the field of computational finance has expanded into virtually every area of finance, and the demand for practitioners has grown dramatically.<ref name=Seydel /> Moreover, many specialized companies have grown up to supply computational finance software and services.<ref name=Goodkin />
